index.meta.title: Rumi in South African languages
index.meta.subtitle: What we measured in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho, with Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana also tested.
index.meta.dateline: Measured 7 October 2026 · every number is labelled measured, AI-judged or native ear pending

index.answer.heading: The answer
index.answer.lead: Yes, with three conditions. On automated tests Rumi reads the curriculum, plans and voices lessons, transcribes speech and drafts coaching in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho. No native speaker has checked a word yet.
bullets: Lesson plans and coaching are strong in all three languages; listening is the capability that separates them.
Today's production transcription engine fails every Bantu language we tried; the engines that work are named on each page.
Every score is machine-measured. One first-language reviewer per language turns "pending" into a number within a week.
index.answer.table_note: Scores are out of 10 and never round up. Click any cell to go to its evidence.
index.answer.native_ear: Native ear pending on every row: no first-language speaker has rated anything on this site.

index.method.heading: How we tested
index.method.lead: Two pipelines, six languages, English alongside as the control; every score compares Rumi's output with a known-good reference by script.
bullets: Curriculum page to lesson plan: a vision model reads the official CAPS pages and the Department's Grade 1 workbook [[fn:fn-caps-zu]] [[fn:fn-wb-zu]]; a planner cuts Term 1 into fifty traceable days; a writer drafts and voices each lesson in the structured format partners use [[fn:fn-rti]].

Classroom recording to coaching report: the best transcription engine writes the transcript; the coaching engine reads it against the partners' coaching course [[fn:fn-coaching-course]], quotes a timed moment for every step it credits, and drafts the debrief.

Three labels. Measured: a script compared our output with the reference (the PDF's own text, human transcripts [[fn:fn-fleurs]] [[fn:fn-nchlt]], the lesson transcript, the spoken script). AI-judged: a second model or engine judged it; it never decides a verdict. Native ear pending: everything, today.
index.method.verdict_rule: GREEN: every test run scored 7 or more. AMBER: one landed between 4 and 7. RED: one fell below 4. Rounding always goes against us: scores are cut down, error rates up.
index.method.samples: Feasibility-sized samples, not a benchmark: 19 full lesson plans and 6 two-week overviews; 143 curriculum, workbook and reader pages; 32 to 70 read sentences per language with human transcripts; 12 classroom recordings (3 partner, 9 public); 6 spoken sentences per voice.
index.method.limits: Listening scores come from read speech in quiet rooms: an upper bound for a Grade 1 classroom. The World Bank structure check [[fn:fn-wb-tool]] tests structure our template enforces, so it sits beside the lesson-plan score, not in it.

index.also_tested.heading: Also tested
index.also_tested.lead: Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana ran the same tests without a page of their own; coaching was not run for Afrikaans and Setswana because no classroom recording was sourced.

lines.nso: Sepedi (Funda Wande's Limpopo language; not Sesotho): lesson plans 9.8, listening 7.8, coaching 9.3 on one public reading lesson [[fn:fn-video-nso]], speaking 8.9. The two transcription engines disagree most here (19.0% to 36.6% of classroom characters across two public lessons [[fn:fn-video-nso]] [[fn:fn-video-nso-2]], AI-judged), so the agreement gate matters most.
lines.af: Afrikaans: lesson plans 9.7, listening 9.1, speaking 9.6. The one language where today's production engine and a first-language voice already work; no routing change needed.
lines.tn: Setswana: lesson plans 9.9, listening 8.9, speaking 9.1. The winning engine is fragile on longer audio, so the runner-up is the safer choice; the voice is intelligibility-uncertain until a native ear decides.

index.also_tested.note: Sesotho and Setswana listening is scored on short read phone prompts with their own South African English control [[fn:fn-nchlt]], not the sentence set used for the other four [[fn:fn-fleurs]]; the two are not comparable.

index.scheme.heading: Scheme of studies for one book
index.scheme.lead: The planner turned one Department of Basic Education workbook into a week-by-week scheme that traces every lesson to its curriculum requirement; the full sheet is open to anyone.
bullets: The six CAPS Home Language editions are one document in six languages (same sections, same Term 1 tables, same time tables); one configuration per language turned all six into requirement lists.
Where the official PDFs contain arithmetic slips, such as a group-reading allocation that exceeds the day, the sheet flags them instead of inheriting them.

The workbook introduces its first letter in week 4; our plans start single sounds in week 1, within the curriculum's one-to-two new sounds a week. The sheet shows the workbook page on every week so the gap is visible.

index.ship.heading: What it would take to ship
index.ship.lead: The infrastructure work is small and known. The expensive part is human: one first-language reviewer per language for about an hour.
rows: Route transcription to the engines that won here, with a two-engine agreement gate so a transcription slip can never become a coaching question
Review the flagged lesson phrases (about seventy across six languages), one transcript and one voice note
one Foundation Phase teacher or coach per language, about an hour
Record one consented three-minute clip per language so Rumi speaks in a South African coach's own voice
Share classroom recordings and structured lesson plans, so coaching is tested on partner material as it was for isiZulu
Share the coaching course's observation tool as used in the field, replacing our synthesis of it
Keep the back-translation check in the lesson pipeline; it caught errors the structure checklist cannot see
Make every pilot teacher a rater: one sentence of Rumi's voice, then a tick, a cross or a "say it right" reply

index.partners.heading: What the partners can give us
index.partners.lead: Four things, in order of how much each moves the numbers.
bullets: Native-speaker ratings: an hour each from an isiZulu, isiXhosa, Sesotho, Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana teacher or coach.
A coach's voice: one consented three-minute recording per language.
Classroom recordings and structured lesson plans in isiXhosa, Sesotho and Sepedi; one Afrikaans recording would complete the table.
The coaching course as used in the field, with its observation tool and teacher reflection instrument, and term plans or pacing guides per grade.

index.cost.heading: What this cost
index.cost.lead: About seventy dollars of metered model and voice calls for six languages, four capabilities, 19 lesson plans, 12 classroom recordings and about 300 speech tests. Authoring and judging ran on subscription seats.

verdict.heading: isiZulu at a glance
verdict.native_ear: Native ear pending: no first-language isiZulu speaker has checked any output on this page.
verdict.lead: GREEN on all four tests, and the only language where coaching was measured on partner material: three VVOB training videos, analysed privately.
verdict.material: Material: the CAPS isiZulu curriculum [[fn:fn-caps-zu]], the Grade 1 workbook [[fn:fn-wb-zu]], three readers [[fn:fn-asb-zu]], a speech test set [[fn:fn-fleurs]], three partner training videos [[fn:fn-vvob-videos]] and two public lessons [[fn:fn-video-zu]] [[fn:fn-video-zu-2]].

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.2: Rumi reads the official pages faithfully, cuts Term 1 into traceable days and writes real isiZulu.
bullets: Page misses are printer stamps and letter-tracing rows, not words; the five uncredited curriculum requirements are taught but paraphrased (twelve-mapping audit).
isiZulu is the only language below the real-word cap: the unattested words are namuhla, ikhanda, amahlombe, everyday words the sources never use.
Fourteen phrases the authoring model was unsure of are on a ten-minute review sheet for a first-language coach.
lesson_plans.note: Beside the score, not in it: World Bank structure check 9.7 (AI-judged, two graders, three lessons) [[fn:fn-wb-tool]]. It cannot tell a good lesson from a filled template: two models' versions of the same day both scored 10, and only back-translation found "first bear" where "first sound" was meant.

vision.heading: Why vision first
vision.lead: A PDF's text layer scrambles workbook pages, so Rumi reads the printed page itself. On this page Rumi read every isiZulu word right; the only differences are in the printer's margin stamp, which a learner never sees.
vision.note: This page: 9.0% of characters differ from the text layer (5.5), all of it the margin stamp; without the stamp 0.0% (10.0). Across all 22 isiZulu test pages: 2.2% (8.9). All measured; highlights count against Rumi even where the text layer is the one that is wrong.

listening.heading: Listening
listening.names_note: Names spoken in the video are not repeated in our text: a learner is [learner], the teacher [teacher], a school [school]. The teacher's remarks to camera are labelled "Teacher (interview)" and are not coached.
listening.lead: Score 8.8: the best engine gets 5.8% of characters wrong on read isiZulu; today's production engine gets roughly every second character wrong.
bullets: Measured on 32 read sentences [[fn:fn-fleurs]] against 1.6% for English from the same set; the runner-up is under two points behind, and a second set of short phone prompts agrees [[fn:fn-nchlt]].
This video has no human transcript, so the two best engines are compared: they disagree on 16.4% of characters (AI-judged), mostly learner names, chanted lists and songs.

One slip mattered in round one: an engine heard a learner's name where a story title was said, and a reflective question was built on it. A two-engine agreement gate catches what quote-checking cannot.

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded here: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found in the transcript (grounding), steps addressed (coverage), agreement across three runs (stability).
coaching.lead: Score 9.6, on three partner training videos [[fn:fn-vvob-videos]]: 97.2% of quoted moments are in the transcript, 93.3% of steps are addressed, three runs agree within 3.5 points of 100.
bullets: The report below is on the public phonics lesson above, so every quote can be checked against the video. It was drafted by a stricter reader than round one's production model, and its own accuracy panel sits under it.
The instrument discriminates: on three runs each, a staged training demonstration and a real, unrehearsed lesson of the same strand came out clearly apart.

AI-judged, beside the score: feedback prose 5.0 out of 10 (understandable, not natural; one judge found an isiXhosa word in it); 21.7% of factual claims flagged unsupported, an over-count that includes evaluative lines.
coaching.note: Given the same prompt, the stricter reader rated the staged demonstration markedly lower than the production model did and named the blockage it missed; coaches relying on the numbers need the stricter reader, or a calibration against it.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.lead: Score 9.6: no isiZulu voice exists on any engine we can reach, so this is an English-accented voice reading isiZulu; it loses 1.7% of characters when transcribed back, against 0.0% in English.
speaking.note: A second listener loses 11.1%, within the agreement band; against human recordings the voice adds 5.8% of error (AI-judged). The listener limits this number; accent and warmth need a native ear.

ship.heading: What it would take to ship isiZulu
bullets: Route transcription to the winning engine, with the agreement gate: where engines disagree on a chunk or a recurring name, describe it, never quote it.
An hour from a first-language isiZulu coach (fourteen phrases, one transcript, one voice note), and one consented three-minute recording so Rumi has an isiZulu voice.
The partners' structured lesson plans as the template's source of truth, and the course's observation tool to replace our synthesis of it.

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.2: the lessons teach the dental click as a sound and read as isiXhosa; page reading is the weakest of the six because one table page was collapsed.
bullets: Half the page-reading gap is a three-column time table whose identical cells were collapsed into one; a quarter is English in a reader's cover art that the text layer lacks, so there the reference is incomplete, not the reading.
The real-word score is capped: a floor test against a reader's own rate, not a ranking. A twelve-mapping audit of the term plan found ten the same, two partial, none wrong.
Ten flagged phrases, led by the model's own description of the click and the idiom for skipping rope, are on a review sheet for a first-language coach.
lesson_plans.note: Beside the score, not in it: World Bank structure check 9.8 (AI-judged, three lessons) [[fn:fn-wb-tool]].

vision.heading: Why vision first
vision.lead: A PDF's text layer scrambles workbook pages, so Rumi reads the printed page itself. On this page Rumi read every isiXhosa word right; the only differences are in the printer's margin stamp, which a learner never sees.
vision.note: This page: 6.5% of characters differ from the text layer (6.7), all of it the margin stamp; without the stamp 0.0% (10.0). Across all 25 isiXhosa test pages: 4.4% (7.8). All measured; highlights count against Rumi even where the text layer is the one that is wrong.

listening.heading: Listening
listening.names_note: Names spoken in the video are not repeated in our text: a learner is [learner], the teacher [teacher], a school [school]. The teacher's remarks to camera are labelled "Teacher (interview)" and are not coached.
listening.lead: Score 7.8: the best engine gets 11.0% of characters wrong on read isiXhosa, the highest error of the six; today's production engine gets about half wrong.
bullets: Measured on 40 read sentences [[fn:fn-fleurs]] against 1.6% for English; the next engine is about three points behind.

On this video the two best engines disagree on 15.1% of characters (AI-judged); across the three public isiXhosa clips [[fn:fn-video-xh-2]] [[fn:fn-video-xh-3]], 14.8% to 28.1%. The agreement gate is mandatory here.

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded here: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found in the transcript (grounding), steps addressed (coverage), agreement across three runs (stability).
coaching.lead: Score 7.6, the lowest of the languages: round one's production model found 92.3% of its quotes in the transcript but addressed only 60.0% of steps, and three runs varied by 12.5 points of 100.
bullets: Measured on this public phonics lesson (the sound "tsh"), with the instrument mapped from the isiZulu course, so its fit is approximate. The report below was drafted by a stricter reader on the same video; its own accuracy panel sits under it.
The coverage gap is real: many evidence quotes came out shorter than the four words we require, so the step went uncredited.
AI-judged, beside the score: feedback prose 2.5 out of 10, the weakest finding on this site; 23.1% of factual claims flagged unsupported.
coaching.note: Re-run on Funda Wande's recordings when they arrive; a first-language reviewer settles the prose question fastest.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.lead: Score 9.7, labelled intelligibility uncertain: the best voice loses only 1.2% of characters on the round trip, but a second listener disagrees by more than ten points.
speaking.note: The second listener loses 14.5%, and against human recordings the voice adds 15.8% of error (AI-judged). A native ear decides; the voice notes here use a different voice for that reason.

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.8: near-perfect page reading, every curriculum requirement placed, and vocabulary as attested as a published reader's.
bullets: A twelve-mapping audit of the term plan found all twelve the same.
Sesotho writes words apart ("Mme o a mema"), which raises the raw real-word rate; that is why each language is calibrated against its own reader.
Twelve flagged phrases are on a review sheet for a first-language coach, led by "O fehla, o fehla" for stirring pap, "hweshetsa" for whisper and the object-less "Mme o a mema".
lesson_plans.note: Beside the score, not in it: World Bank structure check 9.8 (AI-judged, three lessons) [[fn:fn-wb-tool]].

vision.note: This page: 0.0% of characters differ from the text layer (10.0), all of it the margin stamp; without the stamp 0.0% (10.0). Across all 22 Sesotho test pages: 0.9% (9.5). All measured; highlights count against Rumi even where the text layer is the one that is wrong.

listening.heading: Listening
listening.names_note: Names spoken in the video are not repeated in our text: a learner is [learner], the teacher [teacher], a school [school]. The teacher's remarks to camera are labelled "Teacher (interview)" and are not coached.
listening.lead: Score 7.8: the best engine gets 10.9% of characters wrong on short read Sesotho prompts; today's production engine fails the language.
bullets: The main public sentence set has no Sesotho, so this is scored on 70 short phone prompts [[fn:fn-nchlt]] beside that corpus's own South African English control (2.1%); not comparable with isiZulu or isiXhosa.

On this video the two best engines disagree on 25.8% of characters (AI-judged): clean narration, a noisy chorus, spelling turns. The other public Sesotho clip [[fn:fn-video-st-2]] gives 23.9%. One slip in this clip reached the coach: the letters n and g heard as "m" and "kh".

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded here: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found in the transcript (grounding), steps addressed (coverage), agreement across three runs (stability).
coaching.lead: Score 9.7: round one's production model found every quote in the transcript (100.0%), addressed 93.3% of steps, and agreed with itself within 5.3 points of 100 over three runs.
bullets: Measured on this public Grade 1 phonics lesson (the sound "ng"; the teacher says Grade 2), with the instrument mapped from the isiZulu course. The report below was drafted by a stricter reader on the same video; its own accuracy panel sits under it.
A caution the score cannot show: against the other engine's transcript of the same clip only 25 of 42 round-one quotes are found. On Sesotho classroom audio the transcript itself is the uncertainty.
AI-judged, beside the score: feedback prose 5.0 out of 10; 38.9% of factual claims flagged unsupported.
coaching.note: Two failures are kept as evidence: round one's first Sesotho run came out in isiZulu because the output fields were named after isiZulu; and this round's first three runs criticised the teacher for "wrong letters" where the transcript had heard the letters n and g as "m" and "kh". The learners were right; the runs were discarded and re-run once the slip was found, which is exactly what the agreement gate automates.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.lead: Score 8.6: today's production voice reading Sesotho loses 6.6% of characters on the round trip; it is not a Sesotho voice.
speaking.note: A second listener loses 11.5%, within the agreement band; against human recordings the voice was recovered better (penalty -10.3%), which says more about the short, clipped prompts than about the voice (AI-judged). Native ear pending.

ship.heading: What it would take to ship Sesotho
